Easter eggs: a symbol of new life

Celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ. Many go to church on Christmas Eve (24 Dec) or Christmas Day. People eat roast turkey, Christmas pudding and mince pies, give gifts, send cards, decorate their homes and a tree. Young children believe Father Christmas (Santa Claus) brings presents the night before.

Marks the death of Jesus on Good Friday and his rising from the dead on Easter Sunday. Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays. Chocolate Easter eggs symbolise new life and are given even by non-religious people.

A time to reflect and prepare; traditionally a fast, today people often give something up. It begins on Ash Wednesday (an ash cross on the forehead as a symbol of death and sorrow for sin). The day before is Shrove Tuesday (Pancake Day), when pancakes used up eggs, fat and milk.

Remembers that the prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son when God ordered him to. Many Muslims sacrifice an animal to eat; in Britain this must be done in a slaughterhouse.

Football: the UK’s most popular sport

First professional clubs in the late 19th century. Separate leagues in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; the English Premier League has a huge international audience. Clubs play in the UEFA Champions League. Each country has its own national team (FIFA World Cup, UEFA European Championships). England’s only international tournament win was the 1966 World Cup, hosted in the UK.

Games can last up to five days and still end in a draw. Said to reflect the British sense of fair play. Phrases: ‘rain stopped play’, ‘batting on a sticky wicket’, ‘playing a straight bat’, ‘bowled a googly’, ‘it’s just not cricket’. Most famous competition: the Ashes, England v Australia Test matches.

Two types: union and league, with different rules. Northern Ireland plays with the Irish Republic. Six Nations (rugby union): England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy. Super League: best-known rugby league club competition.

Long royal association. Royal Ascot (five days, Berkshire, attended by the Royal Family); the Grand National at Aintree near Liverpool; the Scottish Grand National at Ayr. National Horseracing Museum in Newmarket, Suffolk.
St Andrews in Scotland is the home of golf. The Open Championship is the only ‘Major’ held outside the USA, at a different course each year.
First tennis club: Leamington Spa, 1872. Wimbledon, at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, is the oldest tournament in the world and the only Grand Slam played on grass.

Sir Francis Chichester: first to sail single-handed around the world (1966/67). Sir Robin Knox-Johnston: first to do it without stopping, two years later. Famous sailing at Cowes, Isle of Wight. Yearly Oxford v Cambridge boat race on the Thames.
The UK leads in motor-sport technology. A Formula 1 Grand Prix is held every year. Recent British champions: Damon Hill, Lewis Hamilton, Jensen Button.
Dry ski slopes throughout the UK; five ski centres in Scotland; Europe’s longest dry ski slope is near Edinburgh.

Classical music remains very popular in the UK
From Purcell to punk: music and theatre are central to British culture, with venues and festivals across the country.

The Proms is an eight-week summer season of orchestral music in venues including the Royal Albert Hall, organised by the BBC since 1927. The Last Night of the Proms is the best-known concert and is broadcast on TV.
